title: Agentic AI can already move money faster than banks can watch it
dek: A voice-cloning fraud caseload in Milan, a warning about machine-speed bank runs, and a rush of new guardrails show adoption is outrunning oversight in real time.
body: AI agents are no longer a pilot sitting next to the real business: they are already moving real money, for better and worse, and the industry's controls are racing to keep up. That is the throughline linking a fraud caseload in Milan, a warning from one of Wall Street's biggest credit investors, and a burst of new guardrails from chipmakers, regulators and banks alike.

Start with the fraud. Milan prosecutors now treat AI voice cloning as a caseload, not a one-off. Fideuram's former chairman authorized about $108 million in transfers after a spoofed WhatsApp message and a cloned voice convinced him a law firm partner and Intesa Sanpaolo's chief executive were both on the line. Weeks earlier, the same playbook hit Banca Ifis for about 24 million euros. Both banks recovered most of the money, but the pattern should worry any compliance officer: a convincing voice and a plausible reason to move fast beat internal controls twice in one spring.

Then there is Apollo's Torsten Slok, who argues agentic AI could do to deposits what a bank run used to need a crowd for. Once AI assistants start sweeping household cash out of checking accounts paying around 0.1% into fintech accounts yielding 3.3% to 5%, he says, they will do it all at once, because an agent chasing yield has no reason to wait. That would drain the cheap deposits banks use to fund lending, so a rate gap regulators have long tolerated starts to look like a standing vulnerability instead of background noise.

What connects the fraud and the funding risk is the same mechanic: an AI agent does exactly what it is told, at a speed no human process was built for. So the response has to match that speed. Nvidia's new Open Agent Safety Platform, built with JPMorgan and Citi as design partners, pairs software boundaries with a hardware watchdog that can quarantine a misbehaving agent in milliseconds. The FTC's chair, Andrew Ferguson, made the accountability line explicit this week too: a company cannot blame its agent for what the agent did, because regulators will look at the permissions and controls it built in. Capital One's head of enterprise AI made a similar point from inside a bank: agentic AI succeeds or fails on the data governance and human review around the model, more than on which model a bank picks.

So the question worth carrying into this week is not whether your institution has an agentic AI strategy, most do, or will soon. It is whether you have the callback verification, the permission logs and the kill switch to go with it, because the FTC has already said who gets blamed if you do not.
